segments.narration: Sweden's greatest warship sank after sailing 1,300 metres. The crowds on the Stockholm quay were still waving at her.
Vasa carried sixty-four guns, forty-eight of them twenty-four pounders, stacked across two decks. Enormous weight, carried much too high.
They already knew. Thirty men ran back and forth across her deck to test her, and the admiral stopped it after three passes.
On the tenth of August a gust caught her. She leaned, and water came straight in through the open lower gun ports.
The Baltic is too brackish for shipworm, so nothing ate her. She came back up in 1961, after 333 years, nearly whole.

verdicts.claim: The warship Vasa sank roughly 1,300 metres into her maiden voyage in Stockholm in 1628.
verdicts.note: 90% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 2 number(s)

verdicts.claim: Vasa carried 64 guns, including 48 twenty-four pounders.
verdicts.note: 64 guns total: 48 twenty-four pounders, 8 three-pounders, 2 one-pounders and 6 large-calibre howitzers.

verdicts.claim: During a stability test thirty men ran back and forth across the upper deck, and Vice Admiral Fleming halted it after three trips.
verdicts.note: Summer 1628: thirty men ran across the upper deck; Vice Admiral Fleming stopped the test after three trips fearing capsize.

verdicts.claim: A gust heeled Vasa far enough for water to pour through her open lower gun ports on 10 August 1628.
verdicts.note: The Vasa Museum: a stronger gust pushed the ship so far over that water poured in through the open gunports on the lower gundeck.

verdicts.claim: Baltic water is free of the shipworm Teredo navalis, and Vasa was raised in 1961 after 333 years.
verdicts.note: Waters free of Teredo navalis preserved the wood; the hull broke the surface on 24 April 1961 after 333 years.
